families.s: HSE catering and hospitality risk-management guidance
families.t: employer duties, risk assessment, workers and others, premises, equipment, coordination, emergency arrangements and training
f: Catering and hospitality dutyholders are responsible for protecting workers and others affected by the business.
Health and safety law applies to catering businesses of all sizes where work creates risk.
Risk assessment should focus on the hazards that can cause real harm in the actual workplace.
Main catering risks include slips, manual handling, hot surfaces, harmful substances, dermatitis and knife injuries.
Emergency arrangements commonly need to cover fire and gas leaks.
Workers need information and training on the controls used in the business.
Caterers may need to coordinate with landlords, maintenance contractors and catering engineers.
Premises, equipment and work arrangements should be reviewed when menus, layout, staffing or appliances change.
families.g: Catering risk depends on premises and layout, cooking and cleaning processes, equipment and maintenance, staffing, substances, customers and visitors, training and emergency arrangements.

families.s: HSE catering and hospitality slips-and-trips prevention guidance
families.t: food and liquid contamination, flooring, cleaning, footwear, obstructions, lighting, public areas and prompt spill response
f: Slips and trips are a major cause of serious injury in catering and hospitality.
Kitchen assistants, chefs and waiting staff are among the occupations commonly affected.
Food and cooking spillages are important causes of kitchen slip incidents.
Spillages that create a hazard should be cleaned up promptly.
Risk assessment should consider flooring and suitable slip-resistant footwear.
Cleaning regimes can create hazards and should be planned and communicated.
Drawers, cables and other obstructions should be controlled to prevent trips.
Controls should protect workers, visitors and members of the public who use the premises.
families.g: Slip risk depends on contaminant and flooring, cleaning method and timing, footwear, lighting, obstructions, traffic and public use, supervision and maintenance.

families.s: HSE safe use of knives in commercial kitchens
families.t: knife selection, sharpening, stable cutting, carrying, storage, washing, protective equipment and training
f: Knife accidents are common in catering and often injure the non-knife hand and fingers.
Employees should be trained in safe knife use and sharpening methods.
The knife should be suitable for the task and used on a stable cutting surface.
Sharp knives should be maintained because damaged or blunt knives can require unsafe force.
Knives should be carried with the blade pointing down and stored securely after use.
Workers should not try to catch a falling knife or carry knives in pockets.
Washing and handling arrangements should prevent concealed or uncontrolled blades.
Deboning and similar tasks may require protective gloves and protective aprons.
families.g: Knife risk depends on knife and task, sharpness and condition, food and cutting surface, hand position, carrying and washing, storage, PPE, workload and competence.

families.s: HSE catering and hospitality musculoskeletal-disorder guidance
families.t: manual handling avoidance, task-load-environment-individual assessment, pushing, pulling, repetition, posture, cleaning and maintenance tasks
f: Employers should avoid hazardous manual handling where reasonably practicable.
Unavoidable handling should be assessed and the risk reduced as far as reasonably practicable.
Assessment should consider the task, load, working environment and individual capability.
Kitchen work can cause back, hand, wrist, shoulder and neck disorders.
Lifting and carrying heavy items and pushing or pulling can create back-injury risk.
Forceful repetition and poor posture can contribute to upper-limb disorders.
Cleaning and maintenance activities should be included in the assessment.
Work design, handling aids, storage height and staffing should match how work is actually performed.
families.g: Catering MSD risk depends on load and frequency, posture and reach, pushing and pulling, work height and space, equipment, pace, staffing, individual capability and recovery time.

families.s: HSE catering wet-work and occupational-dermatitis prevention guidance
families.t: water, soaps, detergents, foods, gloves, automation, tools, hand care, skin checks and early reporting
f: Work-related dermatitis is a major cause of ill health among chefs, cooks and catering assistants.
Prolonged contact with water, soaps and detergents causes many catering dermatitis cases.
Direct contact with foods can also cause irritant or allergic skin disease.
Dishwashers and automated processes can reduce wet work and direct contact.
Utensils such as tongs and scoops can reduce hand contact with food.
Suitable gloves should be used where contact cannot otherwise be avoided.
Hands should be dried thoroughly and moisturised to protect the skin barrier.
Regular skin checks and early reporting can identify control failures before severe dermatitis develops.
families.g: Catering dermatitis risk depends on wet-work duration, detergents and food allergens, glove choice and occlusion, direct contact, hygiene, skin condition, surveillance and early intervention.
